title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Candidate's pause call in St. Joseph highlights power, water and land stakes across the state.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're zeroing in on a candidate in St. Joseph County calling for a temporary halt on data-center proposals right as similar battles flare up from the U.P. to southeast Michigan.
Graham, walk us through what this St. Joseph candidate is actually proposing and why it landed today.

According to WNDU reporting, the candidate for St. Joseph County Council wants a moratorium to give local officials time to write rules before any large facilities arrive. The concern is sudden spikes in power bills and water use for residents if projects move forward without limits.
That sounds familiar from other places. How does this fit into the bigger picture of what's happening statewide right now?

It's part of a pattern. Houghton County officials are already drafting zoning and permitting standards to cap power and water demands on rural grids and aquifers before any projects are even proposed. Mason County residents just pushed back hard at a commission hearing over the same issues.
What exactly are residents worried about when it comes to their electric bills and water supplies?

DTE Electric's queue for data-center load has topped 8 gigawatts after deals with Oracle and Google. That kind of demand means higher rates and new transmission lines or substations that ratepayers ultimately pay for. Water use is the other big unknown in places where wells and aquifers are already stretched.
And the land angle? Farmland and small towns seem to be right in the crosshairs.

Exactly. Proposals often target agricultural or rural parcels because they're cheaper and have space for the huge buildings and cooling systems. Township leaders in Livingston County are facing online threats after a viral clip about one such project, showing how personal these fights are getting.
Threats against local officials? That feels like a new level of intensity.
It does. Officials still have to decide on the project amid the backlash, but the episode highlights how raw the debate over power use and land has become in just the past few weeks.
What happens next in St. Joseph if the moratorium idea gains traction?

Other counties are already scrambling to write their own limits before projects land. If St. Joseph moves forward, it could set a template that slows or reshapes proposals elsewhere while giving residents more say on where facilities go and what protections are required.
The Detroit News editorial today urged the state to welcome data centers but only with strong local protections. How does that line up with what we're seeing on the ground?

The board points to electricity costs and water strain already hitting other states and says Michigan communities still have time to write standards. It matches the local push we're hearing in Houghton, Mason, and now St. Joseph.
Any sense of how much power these facilities actually pull compared to what a typical town uses?
One gigawatt is enough to power roughly 800,000 average homes, so 8 gigawatts queued at DTE is massive. That load will shape future rates and grid investments across southeast Michigan for years.
And the money flowing into politics around this?

A super PAC tied to artificial intelligence interests spent nearly $300,000 in a Michigan congressional primary where data center policy is emerging as an issue. Voters decide next week, so the stakes are real for whoever wins.
How are candidates in the Democratic Senate primary responding to these local fights?
El-Sayed and Stevens are both seeking the nomination in the Aug. 4 primary, and the winner could influence federal rules on projects already sparking fights over sites and impacts.
Yesterday Bellevue residents were demanding concrete numbers on water and power use for a proposed facility in Eaton County. Is that the same pattern?
Yes. Neighbors want specifics on how much electricity and water the project would pull, worried about higher utility rates and strained wells if it moves ahead without transparency.
DTE also landed big contracts even after missing earnings targets. What does that tell us?
The deals are driving growth despite the miss, but ratepayers will pay for the infrastructure needed to serve the new load. Those contracts will shape future power rates across the region.
So the common thread is communities trying to get ahead of the curve before projects lock in.
That's right. Early action on zoning and permitting is the main tool right now, whether in the U.P. or downstate.
Graham, what should listeners keep an eye on in the coming days?

The Aug. 4 primary will give voters a direct say on candidates who could shape federal policy, and local hearings like the one in Mason County show residents still have a voice before bigger decisions.
Any other quick developments worth noting from today?
Tech industry money is clearly flowing into races where data center policy matters, and editorial voices like the Detroit News are urging proactive state and local rules.
Let's shift to a couple more quick hits. The threats against township leaders in Livingston County—what's the latest there?
A viral clip sparked the backlash, and officials must still decide on the project amid the online firestorm. It shows how heated these land-use debates have become.
And in Mason County, the commission heard from opponents on power and land impacts.
Local pushback could force changes or delays. Residents got a direct say at the hearing, which is exactly the kind of input that can reshape proposals.
Houghton County is getting ahead by drafting rules now.
Houghton, Hancock and Portage Township officials are working on zoning and permitting standards to limit demands on rural grids and aquifers before any large projects arrive.
That proactive approach seems to be catching on.
It does, especially as DTE's queue keeps growing.
One more quick one—the super PAC spending in the congressional primary.
Nearly $300,000 dropped into a race where data center policy is an emerging issue. Voters weigh in next week.
On deck for listeners, are there any meetings coming up they can actually attend?
The Aug. 4 primary is the big one on the calendar, and we recommend checking the Michigan Data Center Tracker for any last-minute local hearings that pop up this week or next.
Nothing specific on the immediate docket, but the tracker is the best place to stay current.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.
Thanks for listening, everyone. Stay informed on these local decisions—they're shaping Michigan's energy future.

episode_title: St. Joseph Moratorium Push Signals Wider Michigan Data Center Fights
